modes.reason: Fluency and regional awareness develops through exposure to varied target language speech contexts. Students who only hear one regional variety develop a narrow model of the target language.

descriptors.title: Apply grammar and punctuation to compose texts
descriptors.description: use knowledge of modelled grammatical structures and formulaic expressions to compose and respond to texts, using appropriate punctuation and textual conventions
descriptors.knowledge: Students recognise and use agreement patterns, verb forms, prepositions, adverbs and conjunctions (AC9LS4U02). They apply familiar grammatical structures in modelled contexts. They have not yet used past tense in composition, near-future structures, frequency adverbs, comparatives or consolidated agreement across complex word groups.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply modelled grammatical structures to compose and respond to texts — including tense variation, comparatives, frequency adverbs, expanded connectors and consolidated agreement patterns.

nodes.label: Tense variation and key verb structures
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use present, past and near-future tense in composition — selecting the appropriate tense for temporal meaning — and apply key verb distinctions with awareness.
criteria: Produces sentences in at least two different tenses correctly in a composition context
Uses a near-future structure correctly in at least one example
nodes.hinge_reason: Tense variation is the grammatical prerequisite for all narrative and temporal text production. Students who only use present tense cannot produce recounts, diary entries or future plans — core text types from this band onwards.

width.minimum: Compose sentences in at least two different tenses; use a near-future structure correctly; use at least one key verb distinction in the target language.
width.typical: Use present, past and near-future structures in composition; use modal expressions for hypothetical or polite statements; apply key verb distinctions in the target language; apply verb forms for self and others; apply subject pronoun conventions.
wider: Write a narrative spanning past, present and future — using each tense for its correct temporal purpose and explaining the logic of the choices
Produce paired sentences demonstrating a key verb distinction — explaining the meaning difference each produces

modes.reason: Tense accuracy requires repeated production practice across varied temporal contexts. Students who understand tense conceptually still default to present tense under production pressure.

nodes.label: Agreement consolidation and comparatives
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply agreement patterns consistently across complex word groups and use comparative structures to make comparisons.
criteria: Produces three word groups with correct agreement patterns in a composition task
Uses at least one comparative structure correctly

width.minimum: Produce three word groups with correct agreement patterns; use at least one comparative structure correctly.
width.typical: Consolidate agreement patterns in complex word groups; use comparative structures for making comparisons; use ordinal expressions; use a range of connectors including contrast and reason; use location expressions for giving directions.
wider: Write a text comparing two target language communities using at least four different comparative structures
Produce a word group using the same describing word in all available agreement forms — demonstrating full agreement command

modes.reason: Agreement consolidation and comparative range develops through applying these structures across varied topics and text types. Varied production builds transferable accuracy rather than context-specific competence.

nodes.label: Frequency adverbs, expanded connectors and conventions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use frequency adverbs with flexible word order, an expanded range of connectors, and apply appropriate punctuation and textual conventions in composition.
criteria: Uses at least two frequency adverbs correctly with appropriate word order
Uses at least two connectors beyond the most basic in connected sentences

width.minimum: Use at least two frequency adverbs correctly; use at least two connectors beyond the most basic; apply target language punctuation and capitalisation conventions.
width.typical: Use frequency adverbs with flexible word order; use expanded connectors including reason, contrast and addition; apply punctuation and capitalisation conventions of the target language; use number expressions for ordering and quantities; link ideas across sentences using varied connectors.
wider: Write a paragraph using at least five different connectors — demonstrating range across additive, contrastive, causal and temporal types
Revise a simple text by adding frequency adverbs and expanded connectors — compare before and after, explaining how each addition changes precision

modes.reason: Connector and adverb range develops through producing varied text types. Different text purposes draw on different connector types — narrative, argument and description each require different connective resources.

descriptors.title: Compare target language and English structures using metalanguage
descriptors.description: compare some target language structures and features with those of English, using some familiar metalanguage
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise familiar target language features and compare with English using grammatical metalanguage (AC9LS4U03). They apply metalanguage to grammar comparison. They have not yet compared grammatical features in text production contexts, analysed persuasive language effects, or explored informal and youth language varieties.
descriptors.endpoint: Students compare target language and English language structures and features using metalanguage — including text-type conventions, persuasive language, informal variety and vocabulary pattern connections.

nodes.label: Comparing grammatical structures and text conventions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare grammatical structures and text conventions across the target language and English using metalanguage — identifying what each language does differently and explaining it.
criteria: Uses at least three metalanguage terms accurately in comparing target language and English grammatical features
Identifies at least one text convention that differs between the target language and English
nodes.hinge_reason: Metalanguage precision for grammatical comparison is the analytical tool for all subsequent language analysis. Students who use metalanguage loosely cannot engage in the text evaluation and analysis work at subsequent bands.

width.minimum: Compare at least three grammatical features across the target language and English using metalanguage; identify at least one text convention that differs.
width.typical: Use metalanguage in both languages; recognise grammatical elements associated with specific text types; compare traditional text conventions across the two languages; compare subject-predicate structure and word order; compile comparison graphic organisers.
wider: Create a bilingual grammar comparison chart covering at least five features — each with a target language example, an English example and an explanation of the difference
Analyse a target language and English text of the same type side by side — use metalanguage to annotate every grammatical difference

modes.reason: Metalanguage precision develops through repeated application across multiple texts and comparison tasks before it becomes a reliable analytical tool.

nodes.label: Persuasive language, informal varieties and vocabulary patterns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and compare persuasive language in target language and English texts, and explore informal language varieties and vocabulary patterns.
criteria: Identifies at least two persuasive language features in a target language text and names each using metalanguage
Identifies at least one informal language feature or vocabulary pattern and explains its social or communicative function

width.minimum: Identify at least two persuasive language features in a target language text and compare them with English equivalents; identify at least one example of informal language variety or vocabulary pattern.
width.typical: Compare advertisements and public signs for persuasive and directive language across both languages; explore informal language used by young people in target language communities; compare affective language features across the two languages; notice vocabulary patterns for extending word knowledge.
wider: Create a target language persuasive text using at least three persuasive techniques — annotate each with metalanguage
Research informal language used in target language communities — explain each term, find any English parallel and describe what each reveals about youth culture

modes.reason: Persuasive language and informal variety awareness develops through exposure to varied authentic target language texts — advertisements, signs, social media, informal speech.

descriptors.title: Language reflects cultural practices, values and identity
descriptors.description: recognise that language reflects cultural practices, values and identity, and that this impacts on non-verbal and spoken communication
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify connections between the target language and cultural practices using conceptual vocabulary (AC9LS4U04). They reflect on cross-cultural comparisons. They have not yet explored contact language influences on the target language, examined cultural stereotypes critically, or analysed modern language change.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise that language reflects cultural practices, values and identity — including through contact language influences, cultural stereotypes, modern language change, and First Nations Australian cultural expressions.

nodes.label: Contact language influences and cultural stereotypes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how contact with other languages has influenced the target language vocabulary, and recognise that cultural stereotypes about target language communities are oversimplifications.
criteria: Identifies at least three target language words with contact language origins and explains each
Identifies at least one cultural stereotype and explains why it is an oversimplification
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding contact language influence and the danger of stereotypes is foundational to authentic intercultural competence. Students with a single-community, stereotype-based model of target language culture cannot engage with genuine cultural diversity.

width.minimum: Identify at least three target language words derived from contact or indigenous languages and explain their origin; identify at least one cultural stereotype and explain why it oversimplifies.
width.typical: Explore contact language contributions to the target language vocabulary; recognise that contact languages remain important for identity and heritage; become aware of cultural stereotypes that lead to generalisations; recognise shared linguistic history with related language families.
wider: Research a contact language that has influenced the target language — identify several loanwords and explain what they reveal about the relationship between the two communities
Examine a cultural stereotype about target language communities — find evidence that contradicts it and explain why the stereotype persists

modes.reason: Stereotype identification and critique requires students to move from passive noticing to active analysis — identifying what a stereotype claims, finding contradicting evidence and explaining the mechanism by which stereotypes persist.

nodes.label: Modern language change and identity expression
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how modern influences shape target language change, and reflect on visible and invisible elements of identity expressed through language.
criteria: Identifies at least two modern influences on the target language and explains how each has changed it
Identifies at least one visible and one invisible element of cultural identity and explains how each is expressed through language

width.minimum: Identify at least two modern influences on the target language and explain how each has changed the language; identify at least one visible and one invisible element of cultural identity.
width.typical: Investigate modern influences on the target language — digital culture, migration, pop culture; explore First Nations Australian cultural expressions through song, dance or artworks; reflect on culturally appropriate communication conventions; understand shared and distinct visible and invisible identity elements across cultures.
wider: Compare how digital and social media culture has changed the target language in two different target language communities
Explore how cultural expressions of First Nations Australians through song, dance or artworks compare with those of target language communities — identify similarities and differences in one aspect

modes.reason: Language change awareness develops through encountering varied change drivers — digital culture, migration, pop culture, regional contact. Each reveals a different mechanism by which language evolves.

descriptors.title: Initiate and sustain exchanges in familiar and unfamiliar contexts
descriptors.description: initiate and sustain exchanges in familiar and unfamiliar contexts related to students' experiences, feelings and views, adjusting their language in response to others
descriptors.knowledge: Students can initiate and sustain exchanges related to experiences and perspectives, using active listening strategies and opinion-sharing language (AC9LCH6C01). They can sustain face-to-face and digital exchanges. They have not yet adjusted language in real-time response to others, sustained exchanges in genuinely unfamiliar contexts, used descriptive and persuasive language to discuss contrasting perspectives, or summarised others' views in interaction.
descriptors.endpoint: Students initiate and sustain exchanges in familiar and unfamiliar contexts about their experiences, feelings and views, adjusting their language in response to others and demonstrating active, responsive listening.

nodes.label: Sustaining exchanges in unfamiliar contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can sustain an exchange in an unfamiliar or open-ended context — on topics beyond scripted school and home content — using strategies to maintain conversation when language resources are stretched.
criteria: Sustains an exchange for at least five turns in a partially unfamiliar context
Uses at least one maintenance strategy (clarification, paraphrase, or follow-up question) when needed
nodes.hinge_reason: Sustaining exchanges in unfamiliar contexts is the prerequisite for all higher-order interaction work. Students who can only manage scripted or familiar exchanges cannot meet the 'adjusting language in response to others' demand or develop the interactional flexibility that the Y9-10 descriptors require.

width.minimum: Sustain an exchange for at least five turns on a topic that is partially or fully unfamiliar, using at least one strategy (clarification, paraphrase, or follow-up question) when language resources are insufficient.
width.typical: Sustain face-to-face and online exchanges in familiar and some unfamiliar contexts; use open-ended questions to maintain conversation; use clarification, repetition and paraphrase strategies; use descriptive language to discuss contrasting perspectives on personal topics; contribute to online forums and discussions.
wider: Sustain an exchange on a topic introduced spontaneously by the partner — demonstrate real-time adaptation to an unplanned topic direction across at least six turns
Participate in an online or written forum exchange where the topic and participants are partially unfamiliar — sustain contribution across multiple turns

modes.reason: Conversational resilience in unfamiliar contexts is built through accumulated experience across varied topics and partners. Structured practice with progressively less familiar topics — combined with explicit strategy instruction for when language resources run short — builds the confidence and flexibility the descriptor requires.

nodes.label: Acknowledging views and using persuasive language
nodes.checkpoint: Students can acknowledge others' ideas, indicate agreement or disagreement non-judgementally, and use language to persuade or influence others during an exchange.
criteria: Uses at least two strategies for acknowledging or responding to others' views during a sustained exchange
Produces at least one instance of persuasive or influencing language (e.g. framing consequences, offering perspective)

width.minimum: Use at least two strategies for acknowledging or responding to others' views (agreement, qualified disagreement, or persuasive language) during a sustained exchange.
width.typical: Acknowledge others' ideas and indicate positions non-judgementally; use persuasive and influencing language including consequence-framing and perspective-offering; express views on contrasting aspects of personal experience — home/school, study/leisure; contribute personal ideas to discussions.
wider: Participate in a structured debate or discussion where views must be defended under challenge — demonstrate the use of persuasive language and reasoned position-holding
Compare how persuasive and influencing language is used differently in target language and English conversational contexts — identify where the conventions diverge

modes.reason: Acknowledgement and persuasive language must function across varied discussion contexts — peer exchange, group discussion, online forum — before they transfer reliably. Practising across different interaction formats and partner types builds flexible deployment.

nodes.label: Real-time language adjustment
nodes.checkpoint: Students can adjust their language in real-time in response to others — summarising views, rephrasing for clarity, or shifting register — as an exchange develops.
criteria: Demonstrates at least one instance of real-time language adjustment during an unprompted exchange
Can identify what triggered the adjustment and explain the choice made

width.minimum: Demonstrate at least one instance of real-time language adjustment in a sustained exchange — for example, rephrasing after a signal of non-understanding, summarising a peer's view, or shifting register in response to context.
width.typical: Adjust language in response to interlocutor signals — rephrasing, simplifying, shifting register; summarise different opinions in interactions; request and provide clarification; use digital technology to maintain contact and extend exchanges across time and context.
wider: Reflect on a recorded exchange and identify every moment where language adjustment was or should have been made — discuss what triggered or should have triggered each adjustment
Practise summarising a peer's view accurately during a discussion — then compare the summary with the peer's intended meaning and discuss any gaps

modes.reason: Real-time language adjustment integrates unfamiliar context resilience (node 1) and acknowledgement/persuasion (node 2) into the full interaction demand of the descriptor. The teaching investment is in live interaction conditions — not pre-planned exchanges — that require genuine real-time responsiveness.

descriptors.title: Collaborate using transacting, negotiating and justifying language
descriptors.description: collaborate in activities that involve the language of transacting, negotiating and justifying to plan events
descriptors.knowledge: Students can plan and negotiate with others using modelled and idiomatic language, reaching agreement and resolving differences (AC9LCH6C02). They have collaborated on community-facing projects. They have not yet used justification language in collaborative planning, conducted community interviews, or led events involving external community members.
descriptors.endpoint: Students collaborate in activities involving the language of transacting, negotiating and justifying to plan events — including community-facing activities, peer support resources, and events involving external participants.

nodes.label: Justification language in collaborative planning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use justification language — reasoning, evidence, consequence framing — to support positions and proposals in collaborative planning contexts.
criteria: Uses at least two justification structures during a collaborative planning task
Supports at least one proposal with a reason or evidence
nodes.hinge_reason: Justification language distinguishes collaborative negotiation from simple preference exchange. Students who can only assert preferences cannot engage in the evidence-based, reasoned planning that this descriptor requires and that the Y9-10 discussion descriptors build upon.

width.minimum: Use at least two justification structures during a collaborative planning task — for example, giving a reason for a proposal, citing evidence for a decision, or framing a consequence.
width.typical: Use justification language — reasoning, consequence framing, evidence reference — in collaborative planning; provide metalanguage-supported feedback on peers' contributions; negotiate and justify decisions for events including place, time, program, and participants.
wider: Lead a planning discussion — facilitating justification-based decision making and managing competing proposals to a shared outcome using target language
Compare how justification is expressed in collaborative contexts in the target language with English — identify where the conventions differ in directness or formality

modes.reason: Justification in collaborative contexts requires students to construct and deploy reasoned arguments — not just express preferences. Explicit modelling of justification structures followed by scaffolded planning tasks builds the argumentative capacity needed.

nodes.label: Community interviews and engagement
nodes.checkpoint: Students can prepare and conduct interviews with community members in the target language, gathering information about life experience, migration, culture, or community topics.
criteria: Prepares at least five interview questions appropriate to the context
Conducts an interview using appropriate register and structure throughout

width.minimum: Prepare at least five interview questions and conduct an interview with a community member or peer, using appropriate target language for the exchange.
width.typical: Prepare and conduct community interviews on topics such as migration, life experiences, career choices and cultural practices; use appropriate interview register and structure; gather and present findings; create resources to help others using interview data.
wider: Conduct an interview with a community elder or significant community figure — prepare culturally appropriate questions, manage the interaction respectfully, and present findings for a community audience

Compare interview conventions in the target language community with Australian English interview norms — identify differences in how rapport is built, questions are framed, and the interview is closed

modes.reason: Interview skills require practice across varied participants and topics — the same question forms used with a peer may not transfer appropriately to a community elder or unfamiliar adult. Varied interview contexts build flexible, register-appropriate interviewing capacity.

nodes.label: Planning and executing community-facing events
nodes.checkpoint: Students can collaborate to plan and execute a community-facing event or presentation — organising logistics, creating promotional materials, and managing the event using target language.
criteria: Contributes to at least three planning decisions in target language
Produces at least one piece of promotional or supporting material appropriate to the event

width.minimum: Contribute to planning and executing a community-facing event — participating in at least three planning decisions in target language and producing at least one piece of promotional or supporting material.
width.typical: Collaborate to plan community-facing events — excursions, cultural events, school performances, community outreach activities; create resources for others; produce promotional materials; manage event logistics using target language throughout the planning and execution process.
wider: Take a leadership role in a community-facing event — coordinate planning, delegate tasks, and manage the event itself using target language
Evaluate the event after completion — identify what communication was effective, what could be improved, and what was learned about using target language in a real community context

modes.reason: Community-facing event planning integrates justification language (node 1) and community engagement (node 2) into a sustained, real-stakes collaborative task. The teaching investment is in creating genuine community contexts — real audiences, real events — that require authentic transacting, negotiating and justifying.

descriptors.title: Interpret and analyse texts with cultural and critical awareness
descriptors.description: interpret and analyse information, ideas and opinions in a range of spoken, written and multimodal texts, and respond appropriately to cultural context, purpose and audience
descriptors.knowledge: Students can locate and process information in texts analytically and respond for purpose and audience (AC9LCH6C03). They can analyse perspective and language variation. They have not yet evaluated credibility of sources, analysed humour and cultural reference, identified register variation across formal and informal contexts, or responded with empathetic or critical personal stances.
descriptors.endpoint: Students interpret and analyse information, ideas and opinions in a range of spoken, written and multimodal texts — evaluating credibility, analysing cultural reference and humour, and responding appropriately to cultural context, purpose and audience.

nodes.label: Source credibility and critical information evaluation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the credibility of information sources in the target language and apply strategies to assess and compare information across sources.
criteria: Evaluates at least two target language sources using at least two explicit credibility criteria
Explains which source is more reliable for a given purpose and why
nodes.hinge_reason: Source credibility evaluation is the prerequisite for all analytical text work at Y7-8. Students who cannot evaluate sources cannot distinguish reliable from unreliable information — which undermines the quality and integrity of all analytical and research-based responses.

width.minimum: Evaluate the credibility of at least two target language sources using at least two criteria, and explain which is more reliable for a given purpose.
width.typical: Use target language digital and print sources to research topics; evaluate source credibility using appropriate criteria; compare information across sources; use target language search tools; distinguish between fact, opinion and interpretation in informative texts.
wider: Research a contested topic using target language sources — compare how different sources frame the same information, evaluate their credibility, and present a synthesis that acknowledges source differences
Investigate what makes a source credible in the target language information context — discuss whether credibility criteria differ across languages or communities

modes.reason: Source credibility evaluation requires students to apply explicit criteria — not just judge intuitively. Explicit instruction on credibility criteria (author, currency, purpose, evidence) followed by comparative source analysis tasks builds the systematic evaluative capacity.

nodes.label: Analysing register, humour and cultural reference
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and analyse register variation, humour and culturally-embedded reference in target language texts, and discuss how these features serve the text's purpose.
criteria: Identifies at least two instances of register variation or cultural reference in a text
Explains how at least one of these features serves the text's purpose or audience

width.minimum: Identify at least two instances of register variation or cultural reference in a text and explain how each serves the text's purpose or audience.
width.typical: Identify register differences between formal and informal texts; analyse how humour works in target language media; identify cultural references that require background knowledge to interpret; compare target language humour with Australian expressions of humour; read imaginative texts and maintain a reading journal.
wider: Compare target language and English humour in equivalent media formats — identify what is shared and what is culturally specific, and discuss what the comparison reveals about cultural values
Analyse a culturally-embedded reference in a target language text — explain what background knowledge is needed to interpret it and discuss what happens when this knowledge is absent

modes.reason: Register, humour and cultural reference operate differently across text types and genres. Students who have analysed these features in only one genre cannot generalise their analytical strategies. Varied text type encounters build flexible analytical capacity.

nodes.label: Responding with empathy and critical stance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can respond to imaginative and informative texts with empathy and critical awareness — demonstrating understanding of perspective, cultural context and authorial intention.
criteria: Produces a response demonstrating empathy with a perspective or character
Includes at least one critical observation about cultural context or authorial choice with textual support

width.minimum: Produce at least one response to a text that demonstrates both empathy with a character or perspective and a critical observation about the text's cultural context or authorial choices.
width.typical: Respond to narratives with empathy — writing or performing from a character's perspective; identify differences in formal and informal register and replicate these in own responses; compare cultural expressions across texts; respond to First Nations Australian stories in English in target language.
wider: Write a response to a text that takes a critical stance — challenging an assumption, identifying a cultural bias, or questioning an authorial choice — with textual evidence
Compare responses to the same text across different readers or cultural perspectives — discuss how background knowledge and cultural positioning shape interpretation

modes.reason: Empathetic and critical response integrates source evaluation (node 1) and cultural reference analysis (node 2) into a full interpretive act. The teaching investment is in creating genuine reading and response conditions — real texts, real audiences — that require both engagement and critical distance.

descriptors.title: Interpret and translate across cultural contexts
descriptors.description: interpret and translate non-verbal, spoken and written language to convey meaning in a range of familiar and unfamiliar cultural contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can apply strategies to interpret and translate language in cultural contexts, evaluate translation tools, and produce bilingual resources (AC9LCH6C04). They have managed idiom and literal translation risk. They have not yet interpreted for real visitors, converted register across formal and informal contexts, identified translation challenges involving cultural concepts, or composed bilingual texts for public or professional audiences.
descriptors.endpoint: Students interpret and translate non-verbal, spoken and written language across familiar and unfamiliar cultural contexts — including register conversion, real or simulated interpreting, identifying challenges of cultural concept translation, and producing bilingual texts for public purposes.

nodes.label: Register conversion and cultural concept challenges
nodes.checkpoint: Students can convert language between formal and informal registers for different purposes, and identify and manage the challenges of translating culturally-specific concepts.
criteria: Converts at least one informal expression into formal register appropriately for a specified purpose
Identifies at least two cultural concepts that present translation challenges and explains why
nodes.hinge_reason: Register conversion and cultural concept handling are the prerequisites for professional-level translation and interpreting work. Students who cannot manage these challenges cannot produce contextually appropriate translations in unfamiliar contexts — the core demand of this descriptor.

width.minimum: Convert at least one informal spoken expression into formal written register for a specific purpose, and identify at least two cultural concepts that present translation challenges, explaining why.
width.typical: Convert informal spoken language into formal register for different purposes and audiences; identify concepts that are culturally-specific and resist direct translation; develop strategies for handling these challenges; use dictionaries to understand subtle word use differences; reflect on which words and gestures should or should not be used across cultural contexts.
wider: Translate a formal public text into an accessible version for a target language community audience — documenting each register or cultural concept decision
Research a specific cultural concept that challenges translation — explain the concept in depth in English and discuss multiple strategies for conveying it to a non-target-language audience

modes.reason: Register conversion and cultural concept challenges require systematic analysis of the source text's cultural and contextual demands before translation choices are made. Explicit translation strategy instruction — with documented decision-making — builds the analytical capacity for complex translation tasks.

nodes.label: Interpreting for real or simulated audiences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret between target language and English in a real or simulated context — applying clarification, rephrasing and cultural explanation strategies.
criteria: Interprets at least one exchange demonstrating accurate meaning transfer
Uses at least one clarification or cultural explanation strategy during the interpreting task

width.minimum: Interpret at least one exchange between a target language speaker and an English speaker (real or simulated), demonstrating at least one clarification or cultural explanation strategy.
width.typical: Interpret for visitors or in simulated interpreting scenarios; apply clarification and rephrasing strategies; explain cultural concepts to English-speaking audiences; compare language and behaviour choices when communicating across cultural contexts; discuss modifications made and why.
wider: Interpret in a complex simulated scenario where a cultural misunderstanding must be identified and resolved — document the interpreting decisions made
Compare the challenges of interpreting spoken language with translating written text — identify specific differences in how real-time interpreting demands differ from text translation

modes.reason: Interpreting competence requires practice across varied cultural contexts and audience combinations. The same cultural concept explanation needed for one audience may not serve another; varied interpreting scenarios build flexible, audience-aware mediation capacity.

nodes.label: Bilingual text production for public purposes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compose bilingual texts — menus, signs, public notices, community resources — that accurately convey meaning for both target language and English-speaking audiences.
criteria: Composes a bilingual text with accurate meaning transfer in both languages
Demonstrates appropriate language conventions for a public audience in both languages

width.minimum: Compose at least one bilingual text for a real or realistic public purpose, demonstrating accurate meaning transfer and appropriate language conventions in both languages.
width.typical: Compose bilingual texts for public purposes — menus, signs, notices, community resources, travel itineraries; develop glossaries to accompany English texts; identify and correct translation errors in existing public signs; apply bilingual literacy for real community audiences.
wider: Identify and amend an inaccurate or culturally inappropriate public translation — explain what the error was, why it occurred, and what a correct translation would be
Create a bilingual community resource with a real community stakeholder — negotiating content and language choices for a dual-language audience

modes.reason: Bilingual text production integrates register conversion (node 1) and interpreting strategy (node 2) into a public-facing communicative act. The teaching investment is in creating real or realistic public audience conditions — where the text will actually be read by a dual-language audience.

descriptors.title: Create and present informative and imaginative texts
descriptors.description: create and present spoken, written and multimodal informative and imaginative texts, manipulating language to suit context, purpose and audience
descriptors.knowledge: Students can create and present texts adapted for purpose and audience using cohesive devices and a range of sentence structures (AC9LCH6C05). They have created community-facing texts and performed imaginative work. They have not yet manipulated language for deliberate effect — through humour, persuasion, irony, stylistic experimentation — or produced extended multimodal texts with developed drafting and editing processes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students create and present spoken, written and multimodal informative and imaginative texts, manipulating language to suit context, purpose and audience — including persuasive, humorous and stylistically distinctive texts developed through drafting and editing.

nodes.label: Language manipulation for effect
nodes.checkpoint: Students can deliberately manipulate language — through word choice, register variation, humour, persuasion, or stylistic devices — to create intended effects in a text.
criteria: Produces a text with at least two deliberate language manipulation choices
Can explain the intended effect of each choice
nodes.hinge_reason: Language manipulation is the defining capability of this descriptor. Students who can only produce functional, neutral text cannot meet the 'manipulating language to suit context, purpose and audience' demand — which is the core distinction from Y5-6 text creation.

width.minimum: Produce a text demonstrating at least two deliberate language manipulation choices — for example, a persuasive structure, a humorous element, a register shift, or a descriptive device — and explain the intended effect of each.
width.typical: Manipulate language for deliberate effect — persuasive structures, humour, irony, descriptive and emotive language, jingles, wordplay; adapt characters and scenarios to new contexts; experiment with stylistic choices; discuss how language manipulation serves different purposes.
wider: Create two versions of the same content — one neutral, one manipulated for effect — and compare the impact of each on a reader or audience
Analyse how a published target language text manipulates language for effect, then apply the same technique in an original piece

modes.reason: Language manipulation techniques — persuasion, humour, irony, stylistic variation — are built through encounter with varied models and repeated experimental production. Students need exposure to how published writers use these techniques before they can deploy them deliberately.

nodes.label: Drafting, editing and stylistic development
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop informative and imaginative texts through a drafting and editing process, making deliberate revisions to improve stylistic and creative features.
criteria: Produces a text through a documented drafting process with at least two deliberate revisions
Can explain the reason for each revision in terms of intended effect or audience impact

width.minimum: Produce at least one text through a documented drafting process — showing at least two deliberate revisions that improve a stylistic or creative feature.
width.typical: Develop drafting and editing skills in own writing; revise texts for stylistic and creative improvement; seek and apply peer feedback; compare draft and final versions and explain revision choices; produce multimodal texts with developed visual and textual elements.
wider: Conduct a structured peer editing session — providing metalanguage-supported feedback on a peer's text and applying equivalent feedback to own work
Produce a portfolio of drafts showing the development of a single text from first draft to final version, with annotations explaining each revision decision

modes.reason: Effective drafting and editing requires students to evaluate their own texts analytically — identifying what is working and what needs revision — and to make deliberate improvements rather than surface corrections. Explicit revision frameworks and peer feedback structures build this self-evaluative capacity.

nodes.label: Extended multimodal presentation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create and present extended multimodal texts — combining spoken, written and visual elements — for informative or imaginative purposes, with appropriate production choices for context and audience.
criteria: Creates a multimodal text combining at least two modes with deliberate production choices
Presents the text demonstrating awareness of audience through delivery or design choices

width.minimum: Create and present a multimodal text that combines at least two modes (spoken, written, visual) with deliberate production choices appropriate to purpose and audience.
width.typical: Produce multimodal presentations using tables, maps, charts, data visualisations; create promotional materials, travel texts, cultural commentaries; produce dramatic or humorous performances; write creative accounts of historical figures or characters; create captions, subtitles or commentary for video.
wider: Create a multimodal text for a real external audience — for example, a community publication, a school broadcast, or a digital production — and seek and incorporate feedback from that audience
Reflect on the production choices made in a multimodal text — explain how each mode contributes to meaning and why the combination is more effective than a single mode alone

modes.reason: Extended multimodal presentation integrates language manipulation (node 1) and drafting/editing skills (node 2) into a full production task. The teaching investment is in creating real presentation conditions — genuine audiences, real purposes — where production choices matter.

descriptors.title: Initiate and sustain exchanges
descriptors.description: initiate and sustain exchanges, related to students' experiences and perspectives
descriptors.knowledge: Students entering the background language learner pathway at Y7-8 bring significant home and community experience of the target language — spoken fluency in familiar registers, cultural knowledge, and informal literacy to varying degrees. They have not yet participated in structured academic exchanges, used the target language for sustained opinion-based discussion, or navigated formal and digital interaction contexts in an academic setting.
descriptors.endpoint: Students initiate and sustain exchanges related to their experiences and perspectives, using culturally appropriate language across face-to-face and digital contexts, sharing opinions and responding to others.

nodes.label: Culturally appropriate initiation and response
nodes.checkpoint: Students can initiate and sustain exchanges in culturally appropriate ways — including expressing preferences, justifying views, and ensuring others are included.
criteria: Initiates an exchange using culturally appropriate conventions
Sustains the exchange for at least four turns including at least one opinion or preference expression
nodes.hinge_reason: Culturally appropriate initiation is the prerequisite for all sustained academic interaction. Students who rely on home register conventions without adjustment cannot participate effectively in structured school-context exchanges.

width.minimum: Initiate at least one exchange using culturally appropriate conventions and sustain it for at least four turns, including at least one expression of preference or opinion.
width.typical: Initiate and sustain conversations about personal interests, hobbies and future plans using culturally appropriate conventions; express preferences with reasons; ensure other participants are included; respond to class discussion questions with agreement or disagreement; clarify or paraphrase teacher instructions when needed.
wider: Compare culturally appropriate conversation initiation and participation conventions in the target language with Australian English — identify specific differences in how inclusion, agreement and disagreement are managed
Reflect on own home language interaction patterns — identify where school target language interaction differs from home use and discuss what adjustments are needed

modes.reason: Entry pathway students need to build a reliable school-context interaction register through repeated practice. Regular structured exchanges — peer discussions, class debates, digital interactions — consolidate culturally appropriate conventions before students can deploy them flexibly.

nodes.label: Digital and written interaction
nodes.checkpoint: Students can exchange information and share experiences through digital and written formats — emails, online journals, blogs — using appropriate format conventions.
criteria: Produces a digital or written interaction text using appropriate format conventions
Uses register appropriate to the format and intended recipient

width.minimum: Produce at least one digital or written interaction text (email, journal entry, or blog post) using appropriate target language conventions for the format.
width.typical: Exchange emails about school, home and social activities using appropriate format; maintain contact with peers through digital platforms; keep a secure online journal documenting highlights of daily life; exchange information about special events and community celebrations.
wider: Compare email and digital interaction conventions in the target language with English equivalents — identify differences in greeting, register, sign-off and structural conventions
Create a bilingual digital interaction text for a dual-language audience — selecting language for each section based on audience and purpose

modes.reason: Digital and written interaction conventions vary across format types — email, blog, journal, social media. Practising across varied digital formats builds the flexible written interaction capacity the descriptor requires.

nodes.label: Responding to invitations and social scenarios
nodes.checkpoint: Students can respond to invitations and participate in exchanges about special events and community celebrations using appropriate social language.
criteria: Responds to an invitation using appropriate acceptance or decline conventions
Exchanges information about a special event or celebration in culturally appropriate target language

width.minimum: Respond appropriately to at least one invitation — accepting or declining — using appropriate target language conventions, and exchange information about at least one special event or celebration.
width.typical: Respond to invitations — accepting and declining in appropriate ways; share information about special events and community celebrations; participate in exchanges about personal and community life with peers in target language communities; share life experiences in face-to-face and online contexts.
wider: Compare invitation and response conventions across different target language community contexts — identify how formality and register vary depending on relationship and occasion
Create and respond to an invitation for a culturally significant event — demonstrating full command of the relevant social language conventions

modes.reason: Social scenario response integrates culturally appropriate interaction (node 1) and digital interaction skills (node 2) into the full range of social communication contexts. The teaching investment is in creating genuine social scenarios — real invitations, real events — that require authentic target language use.

descriptors.title: Plan, transact and negotiate with peers
descriptors.description: engage in activities that involve planning, transacting and negotiating with peers, using a range of phrases, sentences and structures and features
descriptors.knowledge: Students can initiate and sustain exchanges using culturally appropriate conventions (AC9LCH8EC01). They can participate in digital and written interaction. They have not yet engaged in structured collaborative planning, transactional exchanges, or bilingual community-facing production in an academic context.
descriptors.endpoint: Students engage in activities involving planning, transacting and negotiating with peers — including cultural events, transactions, collaborative projects, and bilingual community resources.

nodes.label: Collaborative planning and cultural event organisation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can collaborate with peers to plan cultural events or school activities, making decisions, negotiating roles, and using target language throughout.
criteria: Contributes at least two planning decisions in target language
Justifies at least one decision with a reason
nodes.hinge_reason: Collaborative planning in target language is the prerequisite for all subsequent community-facing production and negotiation. Students who cannot sustain target language through a planning process cannot participate in the collaborative projects and bilingual resource creation this descriptor requires.

width.minimum: Contribute to planning at least one event or activity in target language, making at least two planning decisions and justifying at least one.
width.typical: Plan Chinese cultural days and community events; organise class or school celebrations — explaining cultural practices and comparing with Australian practices; design group projects using research and personal experience; negotiate event formats, promotion strategies and participant roles.
wider: Lead the planning of a cultural event — coordinating decisions, managing peer input, and driving the group to a shared outcome using target language
Compare how community events are organised and promoted in target language community contexts versus Australian school contexts — identify the cultural differences in planning conventions

modes.reason: Collaborative planning requires students to contribute reasoned positions — not only preferences — and to manage competing views toward a shared outcome. Explicit planning task structures with justification requirements build this capacity.

nodes.label: Transactional and negotiating language
nodes.checkpoint: Students can make real or simulated transactions — purchasing, requesting services, planning itineraries — negotiating details and reaching decisions as a group.
criteria: Participates in a transactional exchange using target language to make a request or negotiate
Reaches a conclusion or decision through the exchange

width.minimum: Participate in at least one transactional or negotiating exchange, using target language to make a request, bargain or negotiate a detail, and reach a conclusion.
width.typical: Make real or simulated transactions — buying goods, requesting services, bargaining on price, planning itineraries; negotiate with peers about purchases and decisions based on collective opinions; provide metalanguage-supported peer feedback on spoken or written texts.
wider: Conduct a transactional exchange in a genuinely unfamiliar context — for example, booking a service or negotiating a complex arrangement — demonstrating flexible deployment of transactional language
Compare transactional language conventions in the target language with Australian English — identify differences in directness, bargaining conventions, and closing formulas

modes.reason: Transactional language must work across varied scenarios — shopping, services, itinerary planning, group decisions. Practising across different transaction types builds flexible deployment.

nodes.label: Bilingual community-facing production
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create bilingual promotional or informational materials for community audiences, and produce resources to help others.
criteria: Creates a bilingual resource with accurate meaning transfer in both languages
The resource is appropriate for its specified community audience

width.minimum: Create at least one bilingual resource (promotional material, helpful guide, or community information) that accurately conveys meaning in both languages for a specific audience.
width.typical: Produce bilingual promotional materials for community events; create resources for Chinese-speaking families to engage with school activities; produce helpful guides for other students; collaborate to create displays and performances for school and community audiences.
wider: Create a bilingual resource for a real community need — evaluate it with a target audience member and revise based on feedback
Design an 'ideal school' or community initiative with peers — drawing on research and own cultural experience to compare aspects across Australian and Chinese-speaking contexts

modes.reason: Bilingual community production integrates collaborative planning (node 1) and transactional language (node 2) into a genuine community-facing task. The teaching investment is in creating real community audiences — actual events, real family and community contexts — that give the production task authentic purpose.

descriptors.title: Locate and process information in texts
descriptors.description: locate and process information and ideas in a range of spoken, written and multimodal texts, responding in ways appropriate to cultural context, purpose and audience
descriptors.knowledge: Students entering at Y7-8 can access and comprehend target language texts in familiar registers from home and community exposure. They can identify key information in known contexts. They have not yet applied systematic information-gathering strategies, evaluated source credibility, or produced structured academic responses to a range of text types.
descriptors.endpoint: Students locate and process information in a range of spoken, written and multimodal texts — including evaluating sources, responding analytically, and producing structured responses appropriate to cultural context, purpose and audience.

nodes.label: Applying comprehension strategies across text types
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply listening and reading comprehension strategies — note-taking, key fact identification, source evaluation — across a range of target language texts.
criteria: Applies at least two comprehension strategies across different text types
Locates key information from at least one spoken and one written text
nodes.hinge_reason: Systematic comprehension strategy use is the prerequisite for all information processing and response work. Entry students with strong oral comprehension but limited academic text strategy will struggle to access the full range of text types this descriptor requires.

width.minimum: Apply at least two comprehension strategies (e.g. note-taking, key fact identification, main idea extraction) across at least two different text types.
width.typical: Listen for key facts in spoken texts — phone messages, broadcasts, announcements — using note-taking strategies; access digital and print texts to gather information; evaluate possible sources before undertaking research; read imaginative texts and keep a reading journal.
wider: Evaluate a set of sources for a research task — apply explicit credibility criteria and justify source selection before gathering information
Compare comprehension strategies used in the target language with those used in English academic contexts — identify where the strategies transfer and where they need adaptation

modes.reason: Comprehension strategy repertoire must be built across varied text types — spoken broadcasts, digital texts, imaginative literature, formal documents. Single text type practice produces narrow transfer; varied encounters build flexible strategy use.

nodes.label: Accessing and evaluating digital and media texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can access, compare and evaluate digital and media texts in the target language — including using target language search tools and assessing source reliability.
criteria: Accesses at least two target language digital sources and evaluates reliability using at least one criterion
Identifies key information from each source

width.minimum: Access at least two target language digital sources on a topic, evaluate their reliability using at least one explicit criterion, and identify key information from each.
width.typical: Access digital media in both target language and English to research aspects of Chinese and Australian life; use target language search engines; evaluate source credibility; collate and present information from multiple sources; access social media and traditional texts and express personal opinions.
wider: Conduct a research task using target language search tools and sources — compare the results and perspectives available in target language versus English language sources on the same topic
Evaluate a set of digital sources systematically — categorise them by type, purpose and reliability, and explain which would be most useful for a specific research purpose

modes.reason: Digital source evaluation requires explicit criteria and reasoning — students need a framework for assessing reliability, not just an intuitive judgment. Explicit source evaluation instruction followed by guided practice builds systematic assessment capacity.

nodes.label: Responding analytically and personally to texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can respond to a range of texts with both personal opinion and analytical observation, producing responses appropriate to cultural context, purpose and audience.
criteria: Produces a response including both a personal opinion and at least one analytical observation
The response is appropriate to the specified cultural context and audience

width.minimum: Produce a response to at least one text that includes both a personal opinion and at least one analytical observation about the text's language, purpose or cultural context.
width.typical: Respond to informative and imaginative texts with personal opinions; view and analyse social media and traditional literary texts; keep a reading journal recording understanding and personal responses; respond to First Nations Australian stories; produce structured responses appropriate to cultural context and audience.
wider: Produce a response to an imaginative text that demonstrates both personal engagement and critical analysis — discussing the cultural context and the author's choices
Compare own response to a text with a peer's — identify where perspectives differ and discuss what personal or cultural background might explain the difference

modes.reason: Analytical and personal response integrates comprehension strategy use (node 1) and digital source evaluation (node 2) into a full interpretive act. The teaching investment is in creating genuine response conditions — real texts, real audiences — that require both engagement and critical distance.

descriptors.title: Interpret, translate and convey meaning
descriptors.description: apply strategies to interpret, translate and convey meaning in familiar and some unfamiliar non-verbal, spoken and written cultural contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students entering at Y7-8 have experience of moving between the target language and English in home and community contexts. They can interpret informally and may conduct transactions or conversations across languages. They have not yet applied systematic translation strategies, managed formal register conversion, or produced structured bilingual texts in academic contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply strategies to interpret, translate and convey meaning in familiar and some unfamiliar cultural contexts — including register conversion, cultural concept challenges, interpreting for others, and producing bilingual texts.

nodes.label: Register conversion and cultural connotation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can convert language between formal and informal registers and identify cultural connotations of words that affect translation meaning.
criteria: Converts at least one informal expression into formal register appropriately
Identifies at least two words where cultural connotation affects translation meaning
nodes.hinge_reason: Register conversion and cultural connotation awareness are prerequisites for all translation and interpretation work. Students who cannot manage these will consistently produce culturally inappropriate or misleading translations.

width.minimum: Convert at least one informal spoken expression into formal written register, and identify at least two words or expressions where cultural connotation affects meaning in translation.
width.typical: Use formal register for speeches and formal contexts; convert informal spoken language into appropriate register; discuss cultural connotations of words expressing emotion or social relationship; identify expressions whose meaning depends on cultural context rather than lexical equivalence.
wider: Compare how the same concept is expressed with different connotations in target language and English — explain what the difference reveals about cultural values
Analyse a formal text and an informal version of the same content — identify every register marker that distinguishes them and explain the cultural logic behind each

modes.reason: Register conversion requires analytical attention to what makes formal language formal — not only substituting vocabulary but understanding the underlying cultural logic. Explicit analysis of register markers builds this systematic awareness.

nodes.label: Interpreting for others and managing untranslatables
nodes.checkpoint: Students can act as interpreter for target language and English speakers, applying clarifying and rephrasing strategies, and handle idioms and culturally-embedded language that cannot be translated directly.
criteria: Interprets an exchange using at least one clarifying or rephrasing strategy
Handles at least one idiom or untranslatable expression with an appropriate strategy and explanation

width.minimum: Interpret at least one exchange between target language and English speakers using at least one clarifying or rephrasing strategy, and handle at least one idiom or untranslatable expression with an appropriate strategy.
width.typical: Act as interpreter for visitors — clarifying, rephrasing and explaining cultural concepts; apply strategies to translate idioms, fables and culturally-embedded stories; read bilingual texts and identify expressions that cannot be directly translated; use dictionaries and digital tools to support translation.
wider: Interpret in a scenario involving a cultural concept that has no English equivalent — explain the concept to both parties and discuss the cultural background required to understand it

Compare own informal interpreting experience from home and community with the structured interpreting strategies introduced in this descriptor — identify what is already intuitive and what requires explicit development

modes.reason: Interpreting and untranslatable expression handling must be practised across varied cultural contexts — different audiences, different types of culturally-embedded language. Varied interpreting scenarios build flexible, audience-aware mediation capacity.

nodes.label: Producing bilingual texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can produce bilingual texts — subtitles, translated resources, cross-language explanations — that accurately convey meaning across both languages for a specific purpose.
criteria: Produces a bilingual text with accurate meaning transfer in both languages
Demonstrates at least one deliberate translation decision beyond word-for-word substitution

width.minimum: Produce at least one bilingual text with accurate meaning transfer, demonstrating at least one deliberate translation decision beyond word-for-word substitution.
width.typical: Produce bilingual texts — subtitles, translated materials, cross-curricular explanations for target language peers; apply translation strategies; rewrite lyrics or story lines in the target language; use resources to create Chinese translations of English texts.
wider: Produce a bilingual text for a real audience — evaluate accuracy and cultural appropriateness with a target audience member and revise
Reflect on the translation decisions made — identify which were straightforward, which required cultural judgment, and what the process revealed about the two languages

modes.reason: Bilingual text production integrates register conversion (node 1) and interpreting strategies (node 2) into a full translation act. The teaching investment is in creating real or realistic audience conditions where translation decisions carry genuine communicative weight.

descriptors.title: Create informative and imaginative texts
descriptors.description: create spoken, written and multimodal informative and imaginative texts, using vocabulary, expressions, sentence structures, textual conventions and appropriate characters and/or Pinyin, to suit purpose and audience
descriptors.knowledge: Students entering at Y7-8 can produce spoken and written target language in familiar registers from home exposure. They may have informal literacy skills of varying depth. They have not yet created extended texts using academic vocabulary, textual conventions, and deliberate stylistic choices for a range of purposes and audiences in a school context.
descriptors.endpoint: Students create spoken, written and multimodal informative and imaginative texts using vocabulary, expressions, sentence structures and textual conventions appropriate to purpose and audience.

nodes.label: Informative texts for real purposes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create informative texts — presentations, posters, brochures, newsletters — using appropriate textual conventions and supporting visual elements.
criteria: Creates an informative text using appropriate target language textual conventions
Includes at least one supporting visual element used purposefully
nodes.hinge_reason: Informative text creation with appropriate conventions is the prerequisite for all academic text production at this level. Entry students with strong oral skills but limited formal writing experience need this foundation before extended or imaginative text production.

width.minimum: Create at least one informative text using appropriate target language textual conventions and at least one supporting visual element.
width.typical: Create digital presentations with sound, voice and music; produce posters and brochures for cultural events; write journal entries and school newsletter contributions; develop procedural texts such as recipes, tutorials and instruction guides; create subtitles and captions for video.
wider: Create an informative text for a real external audience — evaluate its effectiveness with the intended audience and revise
Compare informative text conventions in the target language with English equivalents — identify differences in structure, visual convention and audience address

modes.reason: Informative text conventions require repeated production practice across different formats. Regular creation tasks with explicit attention to genre conventions build the formal text production skills the descriptor requires.

nodes.label: Imaginative and creative texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create imaginative texts — stories, songs, role-plays, cultural narratives — using descriptive language, cultural references, and deliberate creative choices.
criteria: Creates an imaginative text with at least one deliberate creative choice
Demonstrates cultural knowledge through at least one reference, convention or language choice in the text

width.minimum: Create at least one imaginative text demonstrating at least one deliberate creative choice (language, structure, cultural reference, or performance element).
width.typical: Create stories about Chinese-speaking Australians; compose songs, jingles or video clips; write and perform role-plays using cultural stories; create original stories using common expressions or traditional literary idioms; produce bilingual creative texts.
wider: Create an imaginative text that draws on a specific target language literary or cultural tradition — explain the creative choices made and how they reflect that tradition
Produce an imaginative text for a real community audience — performing or publishing for Chinese-speaking community members

modes.reason: Imaginative text creation requires encounter with varied creative forms — stories, songs, role-plays, videos — before students can make independent genre and format choices. Varied creative tasks build the repertoire of forms available for deliberate selection.

nodes.label: Audience-aware multimodal production
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create multimodal texts combining spoken, written and visual elements, making deliberate production choices appropriate to purpose and audience.
criteria: Creates a multimodal text combining at least two modes
Demonstrates at least one deliberate production choice appropriate to audience or purpose

width.minimum: Create a multimodal text combining at least two modes with at least one deliberate production choice justified by audience or purpose.
width.typical: Create multimodal texts combining text, image, sound and performance; adapt language for purpose and audience; produce texts depicting intercultural experiences; create works for Chinese-speaking community audiences; develop drafting and revision skills in own multimodal production.
wider: Create a multimodal text for a specifically defined audience — evaluate its effectiveness with that audience and revise based on feedback
Reflect on the production choices made — explain how each mode contributes to meaning and why the combination is more effective than a single mode

modes.reason: Audience-aware multimodal production integrates informative text skills (node 1) and imaginative text creation (node 2) into a full production task. The teaching investment is in creating genuine audience conditions — real presentations, real community audiences — where production choices carry communicative weight.

descriptors.title: Tone, intonation and phrasing for fluency
descriptors.description: use tone-syllables and apply intonation, stress and phrasing to enhance fluency, and respond to and create texts in a range of contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students entering at Y7-8 have developed spoken target language fluency in home and community contexts, typically with regional or family accent features. They have not yet systematically examined their own pronunciation, compared it with standard forms, applied Pinyin as an analytical tool, or performed for formal or academic audiences.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use tone-syllables, intonation, stress and phrasing to enhance fluency in responding to and creating texts across a range of contexts — including self-monitoring, performance, and awareness of phonological variation.

nodes.label: Phonological awareness and Pinyin as a tool
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain key features of target language phonology — tones, Pinyin romanisation, homophone discrimination — and use Pinyin to support pronunciation and digital text generation.
criteria: Explains how Pinyin represents spoken sounds and uses it to check pronunciation of at least three characters
Identifies at least two homophone pairs and explains how context distinguishes them
nodes.hinge_reason: Phonological awareness including Pinyin use is the prerequisite for all deliberate pronunciation development. Entry students with home fluency but limited phonological analysis cannot systematically monitor or improve their spoken production.

width.minimum: Explain how Pinyin represents spoken sounds and use it to check pronunciation of at least three unknown characters; identify at least two homophone pairs and explain how context distinguishes them.
width.typical: Explore the range of sounds in the target language phonological system; use Pinyin romanisation to generate digital texts; discriminate homophones; practise tongue twisters; use dictionaries and digital tools to check pronunciation; prepare a mock lesson about Chinese phonology for beginners.
wider: Research the relationship between Pinyin and spoken standard target language — explain what Pinyin captures and what it does not, and discuss its usefulness for different types of learners
Compare own pronunciation with standard spoken target language using recordings — identify systematic differences and discuss their origin (regional accent, family variety, etc.)

modes.reason: Phonological analysis requires students to examine features of language they have always used implicitly. Explicit instruction on the phonological system — tones, initials, finals, Pinyin conventions — builds the analytical awareness before students can self-monitor.

nodes.label: Self-monitoring and accent awareness
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare their own speech patterns with standard spoken target language, identify differences, and make targeted adjustments to pronunciation and fluency.
criteria: Compares own speech with a standard model and identifies at least two specific differences
Demonstrates a targeted improvement attempt for at least one identified difference

width.minimum: Compare own speech with at least one model of standard spoken target language, identify at least two specific differences, and demonstrate a targeted improvement attempt.
width.typical: Compare own Chinese speech patterns with Modern Standard Chinese — in news broadcasts or other formal spoken models; identify subtle pronunciation differences including regional accent features; practise adjustments; recognise and describe regional accent variation.
wider: Conduct a systematic self-review comparing recorded speech with a standard model — categorise differences and design a targeted practice plan for the most significant
Research the regional accent features of own family or community variety — describe the specific phonological patterns and explain their geographic origin

modes.reason: Pronunciation self-monitoring requires repeated comparison cycles — record, compare, identify, practise, re-record. Regular structured self-review activities build the reflective practice that produces genuine pronunciation development.

nodes.label: Performance and fluency in formal contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can perform target language texts — poems, speeches, formal presentations — with attention to rhythm, tone, stress and emotional expression for a specific audience.
criteria: Performs a target language text demonstrating deliberate attention to at least one prosodic feature
Can explain the prosodic choice made and its intended effect

width.minimum: Perform at least one target language text demonstrating deliberate attention to tone, rhythm or stress for communicative or emotional effect.
width.typical: Perform Chinese poems with attention to rhythm, voice, emotion and gesture; prepare and rehearse speeches with Chinese-speaking family or community members; perform for specific audiences; use intonation and stress deliberately to convey meaning.
wider: Perform a classical target language poem or literary text — explain the prosodic choices made and how they serve the text's meaning
Compare own performance of a text with a published recording — identify specific prosodic differences and evaluate the effect of each

modes.reason: Performance integrates phonological awareness (node 1) and self-monitoring (node 2) into a full communicative act. The teaching investment is in creating genuine performance conditions — real audiences, real texts — where prosodic control serves communicative and artistic purpose.

descriptors.title: Characters, sentence structures and syntax
descriptors.description: use components and/or characters, sentence structures, syntax and writing system features to infer meaning and to compose and respond to familiar and some unfamiliar texts and contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students entering at Y7-8 have variable literacy in the target language writing system — ranging from strong character recognition from home literacy to limited exposure. They have oral syntactic knowledge but have not necessarily analysed sentence structures explicitly, applied stroke order systematically, or used morphological knowledge to infer meaning in unfamiliar texts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use component and character knowledge, sentence structures and writing system features to infer meaning and compose a range of familiar and some unfamiliar texts.

nodes.label: Character analysis and morphological inference
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse character components and morphemes to infer meaning, identify radicals and their placement, and recognise relationships between characters sharing common components.
criteria: Identifies components of at least five characters with explanation of their contribution
Infers the meaning of at least two unfamiliar characters using component knowledge
nodes.hinge_reason: Morphological inference is the prerequisite for independent reading of unfamiliar texts. Entry students with home literacy may recognise many characters but have not analysed the component system — without this analysis they cannot extend vocabulary strategically.

width.minimum: Identify the components of at least five characters, explain how the component contributes to meaning or sound, and infer the meaning of at least two unfamiliar characters using component knowledge.
width.typical: Identify the nature, arrangement and function of components in characters; infer meanings from component analysis; identify placement patterns for specific radicals; analyse how morphemes relate across words; recognise auspicious character combinations; compare simplified and traditional character forms.
wider: Investigate a semantic component family — all characters sharing a specific radical — and explain the semantic or phonetic pattern connecting them
Predict the meaning of a set of unfamiliar characters using component analysis, verify using a dictionary, and evaluate the accuracy of morphological inference across the set
