nodes.checkpoint: Students can use comparatives and superlatives — including irregular forms — and intensifiers to express and nuance comparisons in the target language.
criteria: Uses at least three comparative or superlative forms correctly including at least one irregular form
Applies comparison structures in a text where comparison is genuinely purposeful (not just a grammar drill)

width.minimum: Use at least three comparative or superlative forms correctly in a target language text.
width.typical: Use regular and common irregular comparative and superlative forms; use intensifiers to strengthen or weaken statements; apply comparison structures in informative and opinion texts.
wider: Compare how comparison is expressed across the target language and English — identify structural differences and cases where direct translation fails
Use comparatives and superlatives in a persuasive or review text — reflect on how comparison language shapes argument and evaluation

modes.reason: Comparative structures need to be practised across varied comparison contexts (people, places, ideas, options) to ensure transfer beyond one rehearsed topic area.

nodes.label: Tense variety and temporal expression
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise and use multiple tense forms in the target language — including past tenses and immediate or simple future — to express temporal relationships.
criteria: Uses at least two different tense forms correctly in a single text
Can explain the distinction between at least two tense forms in the target language
nodes.hinge_reason: Tense variety is required for the extended text production demanded in EC06 and the reflection tasks in EC03. Students who are restricted to present tense cannot produce the narrative, reflective or informative texts the Y9-10 descriptors require. This also underpins EU03's metalinguistic analysis of tense systems.

width.minimum: Use at least two different tense forms correctly in a single target language text (e.g. present and past, or past and future).
width.typical: Use present, past and future tenses in spoken and written texts; distinguish between different past tense forms where the target language requires this; use tense variation to sequence events and express temporal relationships.
wider: Compare how past tense forms in the target language differ from English past tense — identify what distinctions the target language makes that English does not require
Produce a narrative or personal account that uses at least three tense forms — reflect on how tense choice shapes the narrative perspective

modes.reason: Tense accuracy in production requires practice — students often understand tense concepts but apply them inconsistently when juggling other production demands. Narrative and reflective texts that require tense variation provide the practice context.
Tense forms need to be encountered and used across varied text types (narrative, reporting, planning, reflecting) to become flexible tools rather than practised paradigms.

nodes.label: Complex sentence construction and cohesive devices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct complex sentences and use cohesive devices in the target language to connect and develop ideas across a text.
criteria: Produces a text with at least three complex sentences using cohesive devices to connect ideas
Uses at least two different cohesive devices correctly in the same text

width.minimum: Produce at least three complex sentences in a target language text using cohesive devices to connect ideas.
width.typical: Use a range of cohesive devices to connect and develop ideas; construct sentences with subordinate clauses, relative pronouns and prepositional phrases; use impersonal expressions and discourse markers to add nuance and manage text flow.
wider: Analyse the cohesive structure of a native speaker text — identify all cohesive devices and discuss their effect on the text's coherence and flow
Compare complex sentence construction in the target language and English — identify where the target language requires different syntactic choices for the same meaning

modes.reason: Complex sentence construction integrates the grammar and vocabulary knowledge from nodes 1–3 into extended, coherent text production. The move from producing individual sentences to constructing cohesive texts is the key integration challenge — tasks requiring multi-paragraph texts with explicit cohesive marking support this.

descriptors.title: Evaluate texts using metalanguage
descriptors.description: reflect on and evaluate target language texts, using metalanguage to discuss language structures and features
descriptors.knowledge: Students can compare target language structures with English using familiar metalanguage (AC9LS8EU03). They have not yet reflected on and evaluated target language texts analytically — moving from identifying features to explaining how language choices create effect, register and meaning.
descriptors.endpoint: Students reflect on and evaluate target language texts using metalanguage — analysing how grammatical, vocabulary and textual choices create effect, establish register and convey meaning across different text types and purposes.

nodes.label: Analysing textual coherence and structure
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain the structural and cohesive features of a target language text that contribute to its coherence.
criteria: Identifies at least two structural or cohesive features in a target language text using metalanguage
Explains how each identified feature contributes to the text's coherence or purpose

width.minimum: Identify at least two structural or cohesive features in a target language text and explain how they contribute to the text's coherence or purpose.
width.typical: Analyse how introductions, summaries, cohesive devices and paragraph structure contribute to text-level coherence; compare structural conventions across text types; use metalanguage to discuss textual organisation.
wider: Compare the structural conventions of equivalent text types across the target language and English — identify where organisation reflects different cultural or rhetorical expectations
Reconstruct or repair a structurally incomplete or incoherent target language text — explain the structural choices made

modes.reason: Textual analysis requires students to move from what a text says to how it is organised to achieve its purpose. Explicit analysis frameworks (purpose → audience → structure → cohesion) support this move before independent analysis is possible.

nodes.label: Analysing how language choices create register and effect
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how grammatical and vocabulary choices in a target language text establish register, shade meaning and create specific effects.
criteria: Identifies at least two specific language choices in a target language text and explains their contribution to register or effect
Uses metalanguage accurately to discuss language features rather than only describing them in general terms
nodes.hinge_reason: Analysing how language choices create register and effect is the core analytical move of EU03. Without it, students can label grammatical features but cannot explain why they matter — the 'reflect and evaluate' demand of the descriptor is not met. This also underpins EC06's purposeful text creation at Y9-10.

width.minimum: Identify at least two language choices (vocabulary or grammar) in a target language text and explain how each contributes to register or effect.
width.typical: Analyse how formal and informal registers are constructed through language choices; explain how tense, modality, vocabulary and syntax shade meaning and create tone; use metalanguage to discuss and compare language choices across texts.
wider: Compare how the same content is expressed in formal and informal target language registers — identify the specific language features that signal each register
Investigate how social media, technology or globalisation has influenced target language choices — identify specific examples of language change and discuss their implications

modes.reason: The move from describing a language feature to explaining its effect requires explicit analytical scaffolding — 'this word is X, which creates Y effect because Z'. Modelled analysis and discussion-based evaluation of choices build this metalinguistic reasoning.

Language choice analysis must be practised across varied text types and registers to be generalisable — register analysis developed only through formal texts will not transfer to digital or informal contexts.

nodes.label: Evaluating and comparing texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate and compare target language texts, using metalanguage to analyse how language structures and features serve different purposes and audiences.
criteria: Compares at least two target language texts using metalanguage, identifying differences in language choices
Explains how identified differences reflect the different purposes or audiences of the texts — not only describes the features

width.minimum: Compare at least two target language texts using metalanguage — identify at least two differences in language choices and explain how each reflects the different purpose or audience.
width.typical: Evaluate and compare texts across text types, registers and purposes; discuss how language change (globalisation, technology, social media) affects target language usage; use metalanguage to conduct and present comparative text analyses.
wider: Research the influence of other languages or cultural contact on target language vocabulary over time — identify specific examples and discuss the mechanisms of language change
Produce a text that deliberately imitates the register and conventions of a target language text type — explain the choices made with reference to the model

modes.reason: Evaluating and comparing texts integrates structural analysis (node 1) and register/effect analysis (node 2) into a full metalinguistic response. The teaching investment is in tasks that require genuine comparison rather than parallel descriptions of two separate texts.

descriptors.title: Evaluate identity and communication
descriptors.description: reflect on and explain how identity is shaped by language(s), culture(s), attitudes, beliefs and values, and how these affect ways of communicating
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise how identity is shaped by language, culture, attitudes, beliefs and values (AC9LS8EU04). They have not yet reflected on and explained these relationships analytically — moving from recognition of examples to explanation of mechanisms, and considering how identity affects ways of communicating.
descriptors.endpoint: Students reflect on and explain how identity is shaped by language, culture, attitudes, beliefs and values — in target language communities and in their own experience — and analyse how identity affects ways of communicating, including in multilingual and cross-cultural contexts.

nodes.label: Language as a carrier of cultural identity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how specific features of the target language carry and reinforce cultural values, beliefs and identity — moving beyond recognition to explanation.
criteria: Explains at least two connections between specific target language features and cultural values or identity
Explanation identifies a mechanism — not only an example — for how language carries or reinforces identity

width.minimum: Explain at least two ways in which specific target language features (vocabulary, forms of address, cultural references) carry or reinforce cultural identity.
width.typical: Examine a range of target language features and explain how each reflects underlying cultural values, beliefs or identity; investigate how the target language co-exists with other languages in multilingual communities; discuss how language encodes connection to place, community and history.
wider: Investigate how indigenous languages in target language communities co-exist with the target language — research the history and current status of at least one co-official or community language
Research how a target language community's engagement with globalisation, migration or political change has affected language use and identity — identify specific language changes and their causes

modes.reason: Explaining (rather than recognising) the relationship between language and identity requires students to articulate a mechanism — 'this feature exists because this cultural value operates here'. Discussion scaffolds and case studies support the move from observation to explanation.

nodes.label: Identity and ways of communicating
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how identity — including cultural background, social role and language repertoire — shapes the ways people communicate in the target language.
criteria: Explains at least one way in which a specific identity factor (cultural background, social role, language history) shapes communication choices in the target language
Can analyse a specific communication choice in a text and explain it with reference to the communicator's identity

width.minimum: Identify and explain at least one way in which identity (cultural background, age, gender, social role, language history) shapes communication choices in the target language.
width.typical: Examine how cultural background, social identity and multilingual repertoire affect communication choices — including register selection, topic choice, language mixing and the strategies used to manage identity across cultural contexts; analyse texts that reflect different identity positions.
wider: Interview or research a multilingual speaker about their experience of identity across languages — document insights and discuss with reference to own language learning experience
Analyse a target language text (advertisement, social media post, political speech) for how identity is constructed or projected — identify the language choices that signal identity

modes.reason: The relationship between identity and communication is only apparent across varied social and cultural contexts. Students who have only encountered one context (e.g. classroom formal language) will not see how identity varies. Varied encounters — including digital, community and cross-cultural contexts — build the richer picture.

nodes.label: Reflecting on own identity as a language learner
nodes.checkpoint: Students can reflect on and explain how learning the target language has affected their own sense of identity, perspectives and ways of communicating.
criteria: Produces a reflection that explains (not only describes) at least one way language learning has affected their perspectives or sense of identity
Reflection connects personal experience to broader insight about language, culture and identity — not only reports events

width.minimum: Produce one reflection in the target language that explains at least one way in which language learning has introduced a new perspective or affected their sense of identity.
width.typical: Reflect on the experience of operating across languages and cultures; explain how learning the target language has created new ways of thinking, new cultural empathy or new awareness of own cultural assumptions; consider the role of the target language in potential future life experiences.
wider: Produce a personal text (essay, spoken reflection, digital presentation) that traces the development of own identity and perspectives across the language learning journey
Compare own experience of language learning with that of a bilingual or multilingual person — discuss what is shared and what is unique to each experience

modes.reason: Personal identity reflection integrates the cultural insights from nodes 1–2 with the student's own experience as a language learner. This is the most personally meaningful dimension of EU04 — the teaching investment is in creating genuine reflective space, not scripted self-description tasks.

descriptors.title: Apply spoken conventions for fluency in familiar and unfamiliar contexts
descriptors.description: apply features and conventions of spoken target language to extend fluency in responding to and creating texts in familiar and unfamiliar contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students apply spoken target language conventions including consonant nuances, sentence-level stress, written doubling conventions and extended intonation (AC9LS8U01). They apply these in familiar contexts. They have not yet applied spoken conventions in genuinely unfamiliar contexts, nor created extended spoken texts for real audiences.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply spoken conventions to extend fluency — including natural speech features, extended sentence stress, and authentic spoken production — in familiar and unfamiliar contexts.

nodes.label: Natural speech features and extended sentence stress
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply natural speech features — contractions, elision, rhythm — and place stress correctly in extended and complex sentences.
criteria: Demonstrates at least two natural speech features in connected speech
Places stress correctly across at least two complex sentences
nodes.hinge_reason: Natural speech features — contractions, elision, natural rhythm — are what distinguish fluent from stilted spoken production. Students who speak only in citation forms sound unnatural and are difficult to understand in authentic interaction.

width.minimum: Demonstrate at least two natural speech features in connected speech; place stress correctly across at least two complex sentences.
width.typical: Apply contractions, elision and natural rhythm in connected speech; maintain stress patterns in complex sentences; develop fluency through tongue twisters, reading aloud and performance; apply spoken conventions in unrehearsed contexts.
wider: Produce a recording of connected speech demonstrating natural rhythm, elision and stress — compare with a native speaker sample and identify remaining differences
Apply spoken conventions in a genuine unrehearsed context — demonstrating that prosodic features are automatic rather than deliberate

modes.reason: Natural speech features become automatic only through high-frequency production in varied spoken contexts — including unrehearsed conditions. Rehearsed accuracy does not transfer automatically to natural speech.

nodes.label: Fluency in unfamiliar contexts and spoken text creation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can respond and create with adequate fluency in unfamiliar spoken contexts — applying all prior spoken conventions in extended unrehearsed production.
criteria: Produces an extended spoken text in an unfamiliar context with fluency adequate for communicative purpose
Applies natural speech features in at least one unrehearsed spoken context

width.minimum: Produce an extended spoken text in an unfamiliar context with fluency adequate for the communicative purpose.
width.typical: Apply spoken conventions in unfamiliar and spontaneous contexts; create extended spoken texts — presentations, debates, interviews, performances — applying prosodic features deliberately; sustain spoken interaction without excessive hesitation or code-switching.
wider: Participate in a fully spontaneous spoken exchange on an unfamiliar topic — sustaining fluency for at least five minutes
Create and perform an original spoken text with deliberate prosodic design — demonstrate that intonation, stress and rhythm serve the communicative and expressive purpose

modes.reason: Fluency in unfamiliar contexts requires encountering genuinely varied and unpredictable spoken conditions. Rehearsed performance does not build the spontaneous spoken fluency that authentic interaction demands.

nodes.label: Performing and recording spoken texts for real audiences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create and perform or record spoken texts for real audiences — applying all spoken conventions with deliberate expressive intent.
criteria: Creates and delivers a spoken text for a real audience using prosodic features deliberately
The spoken text achieves its communicative or expressive purpose for the audience

width.minimum: Create and deliver at least one spoken text for a real audience applying prosodic features deliberately.
width.typical: Create and perform debates, speeches, dramatisations, podcasts, interviews and recordings for real audiences; apply all spoken conventions — intonation, stress, rhythm, natural features — with deliberate expressive purpose; evaluate own spoken performance against authentic native speaker models.
wider: Create and record an extended spoken production — compare with an authentic native speaker text and reflect on every remaining difference
Perform a spoken text for a target language community audience — receive feedback and reflect on communicative effectiveness

modes.reason: Spoken performance for real audiences integrates all spoken convention capabilities — natural features (N1), spontaneous fluency (N2) — and deploys them for a genuine communicative purpose.

descriptors.title: Apply grammar to predict meaning and compose complex texts
descriptors.description: apply knowledge of grammatical structures to predict meaning and compose texts that contain some complex structures and ideas
descriptors.knowledge: Students apply grammatical structures including irregular verbs across tenses, expanded cohesive devices, quantity expressions and adverbial modification (AC9LS8U02). They compose in past, present and compound tenses. They have not yet worked with further tense forms for continuous or recent action, conditional or subjunctive structures, or passive constructions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply grammatical structures to predict meaning and compose texts with complex structures — including further tense forms, conditional and hypothetical structures, passive voice, and expanded complex sentence types.

nodes.label: Further tense forms and conditional structures
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use further tense forms for continuous or recent action, and conditional or hypothetical structures in composition.
criteria: Uses at least one further tense form correctly in composition
Uses at least one conditional or hypothetical structure correctly
nodes.hinge_reason: Further tense and conditional structures are the grammatical tools for expressing continuous, recently completed and hypothetical meaning — all required for sophisticated narrative, analytical and persuasive composition at this band.

width.minimum: Use at least one further tense form for continuous or recent action correctly; use at least one conditional or hypothetical structure correctly.
width.typical: Apply further tense forms for continuous action or recently completed events; use conditional structures for real and hypothetical scenarios; use hypothetical or subjunctive forms where appropriate in the target language; apply perfect aspect forms for completed action.
wider: Write a text using at least three different tense and aspect forms — each with a margin note explaining the temporal or aspectual purpose
Produce a conditional scenario — describing what would happen if something were different — using the correct conditional structure throughout

modes.reason: Complex tense and conditional accuracy requires repeated production practice in varied composition contexts. Understanding the distinction intellectually does not prevent production errors under pressure.

nodes.label: Passive voice and complex sentence types
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use passive voice constructions and complex sentence types — including relative clauses and expanded subordinate structures.
criteria: Uses at least one passive construction correctly in a composition context
Uses at least one relative clause or complex subordinate structure correctly

width.minimum: Use at least one passive construction correctly; use at least one relative clause or complex subordinate structure correctly.
width.typical: Use passive constructions for impersonal and formal purposes; form relative clauses to embed information; use complex subordinate structures to express causation, condition and time relationships; combine structures to produce genuinely complex sentences.
wider: Produce a paragraph using at least three different complex sentence types — identify each type and explain the meaning relationship it creates
Revise a simple text by embedding information using relative clauses — compare before and after, explaining how each addition changes information density

modes.reason: Passive and complex sentence structures develop through encountering and producing them across varied text types and purposes. Each new text context draws on different complex structures.

nodes.label: Using grammar to predict meaning in complex texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use grammatical knowledge to predict and confirm meaning in complex target language texts — including texts with unfamiliar vocabulary.
criteria: Uses grammatical knowledge to predict the meaning of at least two unfamiliar items in a complex text
Explains the grammatical reasoning used for at least one prediction

width.minimum: Use grammatical knowledge to predict the meaning of at least two unfamiliar words or structures in a complex text — explain the reasoning used.
width.typical: Apply grammatical knowledge to interpret complex texts; use sentence structure and word class knowledge to predict unfamiliar meaning; identify how grammatical features signal relationships between ideas in complex texts; use grammar as a comprehension tool in authentic reading and listening.
wider: Work through a complex authentic target language text — for every unfamiliar word, use grammar and context to predict meaning before checking a reference
Explain the grammatical reasoning behind at least three predictions made in a complex text — demonstrating explicit metalinguistic awareness of the prediction process

modes.reason: Using grammar as a comprehension tool requires students to articulate the reasoning — not only guess intuitively. Structured prediction tasks with explicit reasoning make the metalinguistic process visible.

descriptors.title: Evaluate texts using metalanguage
descriptors.description: reflect on and evaluate target language texts, using metalanguage to analyse language structures and features
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use metalanguage to compare whole-text coherence features, text-type conventions, vocabulary patterns and historical influences (AC9LS8U03). They have not yet evaluated target language texts critically for effectiveness, analysed texts that challenge norms, or connected language register variation to social positioning.
descriptors.endpoint: Students evaluate target language texts using metalanguage — analysing language structures and features for effectiveness, norm deviation, register and social positioning.

nodes.label: Evaluating text effectiveness using metalanguage
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate target language texts for effectiveness — analysing how specific language features contribute to or undermine the text's purpose.
criteria: Identifies at least two specific language features in a text and evaluates how each contributes to or undermines the purpose
Uses metalanguage accurately to frame at least two evaluative claims
nodes.hinge_reason: Text effectiveness evaluation — not only feature identification — is the analytical foundation for all critical text work. Students who only identify features without evaluating their effectiveness cannot engage in genuine text criticism.

width.minimum: Evaluate at least one target language text for effectiveness — identify at least two specific language features and explain how each contributes to or undermines the purpose.
width.typical: Evaluate the effectiveness of texts in achieving their purpose; analyse how vocabulary, sentence structure, cohesion and text conventions contribute to effectiveness; compare effective and ineffective texts in the same genre; use metalanguage to frame evaluative claims.
wider: Evaluate a target language community media text — identify every language choice that serves the text's purpose and every one that does not, with metalanguage framing each claim
Rewrite a section of a target language text to be more effective for its stated purpose — annotate every change with a metalinguistic justification

modes.reason: Effectiveness evaluation requires a move from identification (this feature is present) to evaluation (this feature serves or undermines the purpose). Structured evaluation frameworks scaffold this analytical move.

nodes.label: Analysing norm deviation and contemporary language
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how target language texts deviate from conventions to achieve effect, and evaluate contemporary and creative language use.
criteria: Identifies at least one instance of norm deviation in a text and explains its communicative or creative effect
Uses metalanguage to describe the deviation and the effect

width.minimum: Identify at least one instance of norm deviation in a target language text and explain its communicative or creative effect.
width.typical: Analyse texts that use unconventional language for creative or satirical effect; evaluate contemporary language including slang, digital and youth varieties; identify where texts break conventions deliberately; compare the language of formal and informal digital communication.
wider: Analyse a target language satirical or experimental text — identify every norm deviation, explain the effect intended, and evaluate whether it was achieved
Compare formal and informal digital communication in the target language — identify every register difference and explain the social function of each

modes.reason: Norm deviation and contemporary language analysis develops through encountering varied non-standard texts — satire, digital communication, creative writing each present different deviation conditions.

nodes.label: Register, social positioning and language across modalities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how register variation and language choices signal social positioning, and compare language structures across spoken and written modes.
criteria: Explains how at least two register features signal social positioning in a target language text
Identifies at least one structural difference between spoken and written language in the target language

width.minimum: Explain how at least two register features signal social positioning in a target language text; identify at least one structural difference between spoken and written language in the target language.
width.typical: Analyse how register choices signal social positioning, power relationships and attitudes; compare spoken and written target language for structural differences; evaluate how formality level positions the speaker or writer in relation to the audience; apply register awareness to production and comprehension.
wider: Analyse a target language interaction for power dynamics — identify every language feature that signals relative status and explain how
Compare a spoken and a written version of the same message in the target language — identify every structural difference and explain what each reveals about the conventions of each mode

modes.reason: Social positioning analysis requires explicit interpretive frameworks — students need to be able to articulate what a language choice signals about power, relationship and attitude before applying this analysis spontaneously.

descriptors.title: Reflect on how identity is shaped by language and culture
descriptors.description: reflect on and evaluate how identity is shaped by language(s), culture(s), attitudes, beliefs and values, and how these affect ways of communicating
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explain how language variation signals identity and social relationships, and how co-official languages relate to community identity (AC9LS8U04). They have not yet evaluated critically how language shapes belonging and exclusion, engaged in intercultural projects for real audiences, or reflected on language learning as identity experience.
descriptors.endpoint: Students reflect on and evaluate how identity is shaped by language, culture, attitudes, beliefs and values — including belonging and exclusion, cultural change, and personal intercultural experience.

nodes.label: Language, belonging, exclusion and cultural change
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate how language choices create belonging or exclusion and reflect on how cultural change affects language and identity.
criteria: Explains how at least one language feature creates belonging for some and exclusion for others
Identifies at least one example of cultural change affecting language or identity and explains the connection
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding language as a vehicle for belonging and exclusion is the critical conceptual leap that moves cultural understanding from description to analysis. Students who only describe cultural practices cannot engage in evaluative reflection on language and power.

width.minimum: Explain how at least one language feature creates belonging for some and exclusion for others; identify at least one example of cultural change affecting language or identity.
width.typical: Reflect on how language choices signal group membership and cultural belonging; explore how jargon, slang and specialist language create inclusion and exclusion; reflect on how cultural change — migration, globalisation, digital culture — affects identity and language; explore assumptions in daily expressions; analyse how language changes with speakers' age, relationship and setting.
wider: Examine a target language community discourse where language choice signals belonging or exclusion — explain the mechanism and evaluate the social implications
Research how a significant cultural change has shifted language or identity in a target language community — explain the before and after, and what the shift reveals about the community's values

modes.reason: Belonging and exclusion analysis requires explicit evaluative frameworks — not only descriptive observation. Students need to articulate the mechanism by which language creates inclusion or exclusion.

nodes.label: Intercultural engagement and community projects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can engage in intercultural projects for real community audiences — exploring cultural knowledge and connections through genuine target language interaction.
criteria: Contributes meaningfully to a community intercultural project using the target language
Reflects specifically on the cultural exchange dimension — not only the language production

width.minimum: Contribute meaningfully to a community intercultural project using the target language — reflecting on the cultural exchange dimension.
width.typical: Participate in cultural exchanges with target language community peers; engage in pen-pal and collaborative project work; explore how Australians of target language community background navigate dual cultural identities; produce materials for cultural knowledge exchange; participate in reciprocal cultural sharing projects.
wider: Conduct a genuine intercultural exchange with a target language community peer — reflect on what was learned about both cultures from the exchange
Explore the experience of Australians who identify with both Australian and target language community backgrounds — present findings with cultural analysis in the target language

modes.reason: Intercultural community projects integrate all prior cultural understanding — belonging and exclusion (N1), language and identity — in a genuine exchange with real stakes and real cultural participants.

nodes.label: Reflecting on language learning as identity experience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can reflect on their own language learning experience as an identity experience — examining how learning a new language changes who they are and how they communicate.
criteria: Reflects on at least two ways that learning the target language has changed how they communicate or see the world
Connects specific language learning experiences to broader insights about identity and cultural understanding

width.minimum: Reflect on at least two ways that learning the target language has changed how they communicate or see the world.
width.typical: Reflect on the experience of moving between languages and cultures; consider the identity implications of being a language learner and a bilingual communicator; explore how language learning has changed their perspective on their own language; reflect on what intercultural competence means personally; consider future use of the target language.
wider: Write a reflective essay on the identity dimensions of their target language learning journey — connecting specific experiences to broader insights about language and identity
Consider how their experience as a language learner gives them specific insight into what it means to navigate between languages and cultures — and what this insight could offer in future contexts

modes.reason: Genuine personal reflection on language learning as identity requires students to move from reporting what they did to interpreting what it meant. Structured reflection frameworks scaffold the evaluative move from observation to interpretation.
